sources.title: STAR WARS: Galactic Racer — Crashing with Consequence in Runs-Based Racing
sources.text: Allow us to set the scene. Three corners from the finish line, another racer shunts your repulsorcraft into an adjacent boulder, sending you careening into the toxic wastes of Sentinel I. You try to correct your course. Too late. The vehicle that took you 4 tours and 23 races to tune is now scattered across the track, your League Token is forfeit, and the tour is over. These are the moments that are instrumental in your journey to become Champion of the Galactic League, and the moments that the team built around STAR WARS: Galactic Racer — available today for XBOX Series X|S. “We’ve got a history of trying to make failure fun,” says Creative Director at Fuse Games Kieran Crimmins. “Failure can be this big, spectacular, exciting, interesting and rewarding experience in the game. Our wreck-out system is meant to be the ethos of how Fuse approach game making. Crashing isn’t just a big spectacle; it has consequence as well as mechanical rewards so you can learn something for your next run.” “Failure is fuel, which is where our runs-based mechanic comes into play,” adds Co-founder and Head of Content at Fuse Games Steve Uphill. “It’s the opportunity to try again, and when you get the right combination of builds, parts and upgrades, failure makes winning feel hard earned, but so much more rewarding and creates a powerful and unique player story.” In STAR WARS: Galactic Racer , player persistence is the key to success. Kieran explains what runs-based actually means, and how Fuse Games adds their own spin on the widely used term: “For us, runs-based is a replayable loop that allows you to experiment with a new way to play every time, see how far you get with it, and if you fail, you still get some great rewards to go again so you can try with a new combination of parts and abilities.” “From start to end, the process looks like this: the player starts by choosing which vehicle you want to attempt that run in, whether it be a skim speeder, speeder bike, or landspeeder. They all have slightly different playstyles and attributes. Then, you pick a Racer Style, which gives your build a baseline direction. So, if you wanted to make an afterburner build or a cooled build for example, you start with that Racer Style, then select which abilities, parts and upgrades complement it at the end of each race. Depending how well you do in the races, you’ll also get financial rewards that you can spend at the shop in between planets. There’s always going to be the temptation to try out new abilities or upgrades, but these are rewarded randomly, so there’s an element of luck involved. Most will be able to synergise with your build in some way, so it’s up to your knowledge and creativity for that limited set to find a path to success. If you’re lucky, you’ll win the league. If you don’t win the league, however, the path to success is filled with challenges, rivals, and events to test you. Crash too many times and you’ll ‘wreck out’, or you fail a high-stakes event, then you’ll lose a League Token and be back to the start.” Failure is an important part of the game’s mechanics, which is why ‘wrecking out’ is so instrumental to gameplay: “You have a certain number of crashes that you’re allowed to do in any race,” says Kieran, “not all events have it, but a lot of them do. If you use all your crashes, then you’ll ‘wreck out’ and have to start from the beginning of that tour. Crucially, we wanted there to be an element of consequence in the gameplay. Your decisions matter across every part of the game, so you need some sort of finite failure state for your decisions to matter, and wrecking out felt like a great manifestation of that. Every corner matters, every interaction with another racer matters. It forces you to think about what choices you make and what you’re doing, rather than driving with abandon.” It’s this element of player agency and choice that makes the runs-based loop in STAR WARS: Galactic Racer so satisfying. Kieran expresses the importance of player choice: “If you think about playing in its most base form, it isn’t someone tells you what to do then you do it. That’s a job, that’s instruction. Instead, we provide a play space full of fun things. Play is the choice to arrange them in the way that you want, and creating your own moments and journeys. The power of a good player story is the absolute power of play in general.” And that agency doesn’t end when the run does. Kieran continues: “There are two important progression routes for a run. The first is your stat build-up, where you get temporary stats for each vehicle like cornering, resilience, ramjet, afterburner etc. This allows you to dial into your playstyle as well as your build, and you can add points to make those base stats different. The second one is your combination of parts. As standard, you’ll get to install up to five parts. Each of those parts have different rarity, and you build those up as you go through the different events, either from the shop or as event awards. They all do vastly different things and synergise in different ways, some even develop faults that change builds even further. The combinations in the parts system is so vast, I’m not even sure we’ve seen every single combination yet!” “You also get permanent progression outside of each tour that you can put into one of your vehicle types. So, it’s the same set of stats, but they’ll stay there for the rest of your enjoyment of the game. Once you beat a tour, you open up a larger pool of parts. You’ll also unlock new ‘favors’ that you can equip to further modify the rules for the next run. Another form of permanent progression is the ability to upgrade your Racer Styles, so you can unlock all sorts of different ways to play.” These features carry over to multiplayer, too: “In multiplayer, we wanted to create a runs-based system that worked. sources.title: Star Wars: Galactic Racer Multiplayer Party Limit Will Be Doubled Via Update
sources.text: Star Wars: Galactic Racer has broadly proven to be a smash hit with critics, and fans seem similarly enthusiastic, but developer Fuse Games has heard the concern regarding multiplayer party sizes and has responded via the game’s official social media. Resultingly, it appears we should be able to expect an update to increase the multiplayer party size from three to six players at some point within the next few weeks. “Thank you so much for your feedback and we’d like to let you and everyone on this thread know that we hear you,” the developer responded to various fans raising the concern online. “We’re working on an update to increase the party size from three to six players, with the aim of releasing it within the first few weeks of launch.” More details will be available soon, the developer noted. IGN’s Star Wars: Galactic Racer review called it “a fabulous looking and frantically fast anti-grav racer… that has successfully lit the afterburners on a long-dormant slice of the Star Wars universe.” Luke Reilly is an award-winning journalist with 23 years of media experience across Official PlayStation Magazine, Australian 360, and IGN – which he joined in 2011. You can find him on Bluesky @mrlukereilly to ask him things about stuff.

sources.title: Star Wars: Galactic Racer will double the game’s multiplayer party limit in an upcoming patch
sources.text: The game currently supports parties of 3 players Star Wars: Galactic Racer developer Fuse Games has announced that the game’s multiplayer party limit will be doubled in an upcoming update. At the time of writing, Star Wars: Galactic Racer ‘s multiplayer parties are currently limited to three players, a limitation that was met with dissapointment from players who wanted to play with more of their friends. Now, in a social media post, the Star Wars: Galactic Racer account has confirmed that this restriction will be eased in a future update. Responding to a fan on X , the account wrote, “Thank you so much for your feedback and we’d like to let you and everyone on this thread know that we hear you! We’re working on an update to increase the party size from 3 to 6 players, with the aim of releasing it within the first few weeks of launch. More details coming soon!” Thank you so much for your feedback and we'd like to let you and everyone on this thread know that we hear you! We're working on an update to increase the party size from 3 to 6 players, with the aim of releasing it within the first few weeks of launch. More details coming soon! While no specific date for this update was shared, it should comes as good news to fans. Star Wars: Galactic Racer has been met with critical acclaim and strong player support, but issues like the lack of private multiplayer races, and this small party restriction remain. VGC’s review of the game called it a “modern racing classic” that “absolutely nails what it is trying to do”. “It is a high-octane racer that’s endless fun to play, and it looks fantastic,” we said. “This would have been a great game with a standard single-player mode, but what is here is inventive and engaging. I’d have loved a few silly classic characters and another planet or two, but this is a game I’ll return to for a long time.” Star Wars: Galactic Racer was released earlier this week. At the time of writing, players with Amazon Prime can play the single-player portion of the game via Amazon’s Luna service at no extra cost. “We’ve always believed Luna players deserve to be in the action from day one, and Star Wars: Galactic Racer makes that a reality for the first time,” Amazon head of gaming Jeff Gattis told GamesIndustry.biz in a statement.

stories.title: Resident Evil games engagement leapt 50% following release of Zach Cregger's movie, but analysts say real value is in brand building
stories.summary: Player engagement with Resident Evil games jumped 50% in the run up to and following the release of Zach Cregger's Resident Evil movie, according to data shared exclusively with GamesIndustry.biz . Read more

sources.name: GamesIndustry.biz
sources.title: Resident Evil games engagement leapt 50% following release of Zach Cregger's movie, but analysts say real value is in brand building
sources.text: Resident Evil 2, which like the film is set in Raccoon City, saw a particularly high jump in daily active users Player engagement with Resident Evil games jumped 50% in the run up to and following the release of Zach Cregger's Resident Evil movie, according to data shared exclusively with GamesIndustry.biz . Sensor Tower looked at five Resident Evil titles across Steam, PlayStation, and Xbox, including Requiem, Resident Evil 2, Resident Evil 4, Village, and Biohazard. Daily active users (DAU) jumped 50% from 500,000 on August 30 to 750,000 on September 20. All five games saw increased engagement. Daily unit sales grew from 34,000 to nearly 80,000 over the same period. Looking at the overall Resident Evil franchise, Ampere Analysis found that DAU grew from 140,000 to 680,000 over the course of two weekends from September 6 to September 20. Cregger's film premiered on September 18. There were 540,000 players across the Resident Evil franchise on Sunday, September 6, which increased 11% to 600,000 the Sunday following. DAU increased a further 13% to 680,000 on the Sunday after the movie was released. Ampere's data covered 45 countries on PS, 32 countries on Xbox, and 41 countries on Steam. According to data from Newzoo, which was sourced from 37 markets excluding China, DAU across PC, PS, and Xbox averaged 72% higher than late-summer baselines five days following the film's release in most markets (September 16–18), reaching a peak of 282,526 on Sunday, September 20. Karl Kontus, SVP and general manager of Video Game Insights at Sensor Tower, notes that while these increases are significant, they start from a relatively low base "If we take a longer time frame view (last 12 months), these relative increases in DAU and unit sales from the movie's launch are very very small compared to the portfolio's overall performance," Kontus explains. "In fact, if you're looking at the cumulative units sold for Resident Evil Requiem, the movie launch's impact barely affects the game's overall performance." "The transmedia impact is clearly and measurably affecting game performance by increasing units sold and daily active users. We see this with Resident Evil as well as The Last of Us and Fallout," he continues. "However, this impact is typically very small in the context of the overall game's performance – a single-digit percentage uplift to units and revenue. Ampere Analysis' Piers Harding-Rolls agrees: "The Resident Evil movie has had a sizable positive impact on activity and sales of Resident Evil games across consoles and PC. However, while growth has been noteworthy, the actual volumes involved are small. With an estimated 6 million+ tickets for the movie being sold, the impact has been relatively minor in that context." "The benefit of these transmedia initiatives isn't the short-term increase in game sales. It's IP and brand building. Staying relevant in the players' and watchers' minds. It guarantees that future game launches will remain successful." Discounts also heavily influenced engagement metrics. Capcom cut prices across the series from September 8 on Steam and September 10 on consoles, which lifted DAUs by 21% prior to the film's release. Harding-Rolls also highlights that there was a 30% discount on Requiem across platforms from September 7 to coincide with the film launch. However, "in volume terms the impact on sales [on Requiem] has been relatively lightweight." "This recent discount follows another reduction that took place in late May and early June, which is likely to have reduced the impact during this second discounting campaign." Newzoo's data found that engagement across the Resident Evil franchise rose "sharply" during the film's opening weekend, driven primarily by Resident Evil 2. Emmanuel Rosier, director of marketing intelligence at Newzoo, says Resident Evil 2 attracted players because it "was the cheapest way in" to the franchise at $7.99, a sixth of the discounted price. "The pattern suggests the film sends players to the entry point that matches what they just watched, rather than to the newest game." Rosier adds that Resident Evil 2 saw the most activity because the film shares its setting. "The film's director, Zach Cregger, has described the film as a story running in parallel to Raccoon City's outbreak, the setting of Resident Evil 2, and that is where the game players went back to. Its DAU came close to five times baseline after release, up from under twice baseline during the price cut, and rose on all three platforms at once." That's in contrast to Sensor Tower's data, which demonstrated that Resident Evil 4 and Requiem had much more of an effect on engagement than Resident Evil 2. Rosier noted that Resident Evil 2's engagement rate closely followed the DAU pattern of Assassin's Creed Odyssey in July , with one key difference. "Christopher Nolan's Odyssey opened on July 17, and a PlayStation-only discount followed on July 25," said Rosier. "This time, the discounts came first, on Steam from September 8 and on PlayStation and Xbox from September 10, and the film followed eight to 10 days later. The 38% jump from September 18 to 19 came on top of prices that were already cut." Reviewing engagement increases for both Odyssey and Resident Evil 2, Rosier notes that "the game closest to the film moves most," which then lifts the broader franchise. "Odyssey, set in ancient Greece, rose far more than the rest of the Assassin's Creed catalogue. Resident Evil 2, set during the Raccoon City outbreak that Cregger's story runs in parallel to, rose to nearly five times its baseline, well ahead of Requiem, the newest release. Other Assassin's Creed titles rose about 1.4 times from the film's opening, while the Resident Evil franchise total rose 72% after release."

sources.text: Today marks the worldwide launch of Gears of War: E-Day , now available on XBOX Series X|S, XBOX on PC, Game Pass and Steam. One of XBOX’s most iconic sagas returns to where it all began, taking players back to the opening hours of Emergence Day and the catastrophic event that changed the world of Sera forever. Emergence Day is a defining moment for the Gears of War universe – the catastrophic event changed the world of Sera forever, but the story of that fateful night has never been fully told, until now. Gears of War: E-Day transports us back to the opening hours of the Locust invasion, where an unsuspecting world is ruthlessly plunged into chaos as monsters erupt from underground. Across three harrowing days and nights, Marcus Fenix, Dom Santiago and their fierce new squad mates fight desperately to survive the onslaught consuming the city of Kalona, while uncovering the true scale of a threat unlike anything they – or humanity – has ever faced. From the moment the prologue opens, Gears of War: E-Day showcases a masterclass in action-horror. This is not the Locust enemy you’ve fought before. They’re equally cunning as they are violent, and frankly, you should be terrified to face them. If this is your first deployment, or you’re coming out of retirement to fight the war ahead, we’ve got you covered. Before you step out onto the streets of Kalona, here are a few things every Gear should know. Gears of War is famously a cover-based shooter, and you’ll rely on it to stay alive as you push through the Locust. Keep your head down and dip from cover-to-cover – and avoid walking out into the open unless you’re rushing an enemy with a melee attack. Even a handful of Drones can deal massive damage while you’re exposed, which can be trouble for both you and the squadmate that may have to come and revive you. Sometimes, the best course of action is to hold patiently and pick off enemies as they come, and there’s no shame in that strategy. Sometimes, you’ll just need to haul ass and stay as mobile as you can, which I quickly learned during an early fight with a Brumak wielding a horrible chain weapon. There’s no peace to be found in cover for that situation – fan out, keep it distracted, and pray that it doesn’t decide to charge you while your gun is jammed. Each weapon you’ll find in E-Day is deeply situational, which makes for a great tactical experience. The Chainsaw Lancer is a great all-rounder, offering close-to-mid range firepower and a big ol’ (upgradeable) mag to chew through. The Gnasher is a stellar shotgun, fantastic for devastating point-blank damage. The Longshot Sniper, one of my personal favorites, pops a slick, long-range slug into unsuspecting foes from a great distance. Not only is that incredibly satisfying each time, but it lets you get a stack of damage into a tankier enemy – like a Boomer, before it gets close to you. There are caches dotted around Kalona that let you switch up your loadout, too, so don’t feel like you’re locked into a specific style of play forever. Mix up your strategy, swap roles with your friends, but above all – experiment! I know I said this is a cover-based shooter, but sometimes you’ll need to resort to more personal measures. Before E-Day even lets you look at a gun, it hands out a crash course in melee – one of the most useful, life-saving abilities for a Gear. Spend some time getting to grips with how it works when wielding a metal pipe and the Snub pistol – figure out the weight of the swing, and how it feels to hit enemies in front, and more importantly, behind you. Later, melee becomes even more fun with the Chainsaw Lancer, and you’ll feel extra confident with it once you’ve got the basics of backhanding down. As soon as you pop your head up to aim a shot, you’re a giant bullet magnet, effectively inviting every weapon-wielder on the map to pop you like a balloon. Fortunately, Gears can shoot blind from behind cover, which is a superb way to dish out additional damage to something getting too close for comfort. If you don’t have the health to rush out for a melee takedown, or you need a few seconds of recovery time, blind fire from cover is a clutch move to get the job done. While E-Day ‘s campaign is primarily linear, Kalona has large pockets of open space with multiple pathways towards the next objective, as well as side paths that may lead to side missions. These are smaller, optional objectives that let you support other squads, help civilians, and otherwise contribute to saving the city. Not only do they offer additional insight into the wider story, you’ll also get a nice reward for doing it, often a weapon mod. While you’re exploring, keep an ear open for a sharp chime whenever you enter a new area of the city – anywhere from inside a building to a side street. That means there’s a collectable nearby. These range from familiar items like COG armor and tags, to esoteric pieces like… a can of soup. They all come with great little lore entries too, some written by the squad members themselves. It’s a wonderful added insight into their stories, and the wider world, so pick them up when you can. Now that you’re equipped with the basics, there’s only one thing left to do – get out there. Gather your squad, load up, and uncover the world-shattering event that started it all. Gears of War: E-Day is available today on XBOX Series X|S, XBOX on PC, Game Pass and Steam. Play it on both console and PC at no additional cost with XBOX Play Anywhere.

sources.title: Gears of War E-Day Is a 'Natural Choice to Be an Exclusive' – Studio Head Mike Crump Claims Series Carries the Banner for Xbox
sources.text: Gears of War: E-Day launched this week, and while it is excellent, the game was pulled away from a PS5 launch earlier this year. In a recent interview, The Coalition Studio Head Mike Crump claims that this was all part of the plan. In an interview with the BBC , Crump defended the choice to be an Xbox exclusive, despite a likely ludicrous budget saying, "Gears has been an exclusive franchise to Xbox for 20 years now. It's sort of entwined deeply with the brand." However, Gears of War: Reloaded did launch on PS5 last year, so the franchise as a whole isn't exactly Xbox-exclusive anymore. It's also likely that if E-Day did launch on PlayStation, it'd see higher sales numbers. Crump claims that the metrics for success go further than that, though. He told the BBC that the series is meant to, at least in part, carry the banner for the Xbox platform and give people a "reason to be in the Xbox ecosystem." Queue Xbox CEO Asha Sharma's decision to pull the game from the PS5 release slate. Regardless, the game will now likely have lower sales than it otherwise would have. When the BBC asked Crump about that, he insisted that the studio is taking a broader view than just looking at sales figures and retention numbers. "We measure things like, are we showcasing the platform? Are we pushing the hardware to it limits? Are we showcasing what the Xbox is capable of? ...Our goal basically is to be the best-looking game on the Xbox and really show the industry what's possible with our hardware," he answered. If the goal is to be a tech demo about what the Xbox consoles are capable of, I'd argue that it's a straight-up success. The game looks incredible on both the Xbox Series X and Series S, so much so that The Coalition had to rely on trickery with the Page File to get the game running smoothly on the less-powerful console. The game is also incredible, and our reviewer Ryan McCaffrey gave it a 9 , saying: "By going back to the beginning, Gears of War: E-Day returns to the heart of this series: Marcus Fenix, Dom Santiago, and a Locust horde that’s as terrifying as it is dangerous. E-Day pulls off the tightrope act of giving us a heartfelt prequel with strong characters even when we know how it ends. On a more mechanical level, it also evolves the enemies, weapons, and combat you’d expect to deliver a Gears of War campaign that stands toe-to-toe with any of the others. It wraps up with 10 years still left to go before Marcus gets tossed in prison ahead of the events of the first Gears of War, so here’s hoping the next one stays in the past for a while longer – and that we don’t have to wait another seven years for it to arrive." But even if the game is a critical hit and a technical marvel, sales numbers will inevitably play a role in the game's success, especially as Microsoft is currently in the middle of a months-long restructuring campaign. Right after launch, developers at The Coalition told Eurogamer they were expecting layoffs. However, Crump has since addressed those concerns , saying, "For us that's about shipping a great game that people are going to love and I feel like, as a team, we've done that." Let's just hope that a pretty game and high review scores really are enough to keep the Xbox layoff machine at bay. Jackie Thomas is the Senior Tech Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. sources.title: Undead Labs speaks about its split from Xbox, revealing it has to "make some changes" to State of Decay 3 following layoffs
sources.text: Parting with colleagues was "total heartbreak". State of Decay studio Undead Labs has spoken out after rebuying its independence and leaving Xbox last month, revealing it has "got to make some changes" to State of Decay 3 because of layoffs it suffered as a result. Studio boss Phillip Holt said this during a wide-ranging conversation with The Game Business , in which he detailed the studio's shifting priorities now it has no "boss" to respond to other than its audience, and while explaining why the co-op zombie survival game seems to have been in development for ages. "We're pretty close to finishing this game," Holt said. "And there's a lot in it. I think folks that saw us at Gamescom can attest to that. I think our alpha players can attest to that. And obviously, with a significant number of people leaving the company, we've got to make some changes. But I don't think we're dramatically addressing scope in that way." State of Decay 3 currently has a vague release date of "2027" , announced this summer, which allows Undead Labs some scheduling wiggle-room. But the game was originally revealed all the way back in 2020 , before slipping out of view for a long time, leading people to wonder about what was going on. "I don't think it's taken that long, actually," Holt remarked, when speaking about the game's long development. "If you measure it from when State of Decay 2 shipped, yeah, we're approaching eight years. If you measure it from our first trailer with the infamous zombie deer, that's also a long time. I got myself in a little bit of trouble by saying we didn't really have a team working on the game at that point, which wasn't entirely true, we had a very small team. We've had a small team on the game since maybe 2020. But development didn't really pick up until 2022 or 2023." But why did Undead Labs announce the third State of Decay game so early? The answer is eerily prophetic, and it's to do with the spending spree Microsoft was on when it acquired Undead Labs in 2018 - the same spending spree that saw it acquire Ninja Theory, Compulsion Games, and Playground Games (two of which are also no longer a part of Xbox). Holt wanted to announce State of Decay 3 before Undead Labs was "swallowed up or divested" by the rest of a much bigger gaming division, he said. "I didn't think Microsoft was done being acquisitive," Holt explained, "and I didn't think they'd continue buying small developers - I assumed they'd start buying big things. I was a little worried about getting swallowed up or divested before we had a chance to present to the world what we were working on. So, it was a bit of a marker on the table. I was saying, 'State of Decay 3, we're announcing it, the audience knows it's in development, and here's a trailer to demonstrate our vision.'" Undead Labs was eventually earmarked for divestiture this summer when Xbox announced its major restructuring . At the time, Undead Labs was said to have "entered terms to join new ownership", but that new-ownership deal - as in the case of Ninja Theory - never actually materialised. "We had a lot of interest," Holt assured The Game Business, but when he heard other studios were doing management buyouts, he submitted one for Undead Labs, "and Microsoft thought that would be a good idea". Holt wouldn't say how many people were laid off as a result of the studio downsizing to operate independently, "because these are our friends and colleagues and it was a total heartbreak to have to part ways". "I would hate to reduce the impact to those individuals to a number or statistic," he said. But he insisted the studio had "everything we need to ship State of Decay 3", and that its mission was now even clearer. "Inside of a larger company, you serve multiple objectives and you have directives that you need to achieve," Holt said. "Now it's just: make the best possible game. Of course, inside Xbox, that was also the primary objective. But it's just a cleaner, clearer line of sight to the audience. I don't have a boss. The success or failure of the company is down to whether we create something an audience will support.” State of Decay 3 will still launch on Game Pass on day one, and Holt praised Xbox's subscription service as being partly responsible for the series' ongoing success, which has apparently seen it reach 25 million players over its lifetime. "I don't know that we'd be in the place we are today if not for the Game Pass audience," he acknowledged. "Even today, we have several thousand people coming through the door every day." Dom had a chance to play State of Decay 3 and echoed what Holt said above, that the game was looking good. They're hoping to find some time to write more fully about it soon. sources.text: Google Playground is a browser-based tool for making games from AI prompts. Google Playground is a browser-based tool for making games from AI prompts. Google today announced Playground, a new browser-based platform for making custom games from AI prompts. Playground will be available today in the US for users who are 18 and older at playground.google. The company is pitching it as an “experimental gaming platform” that “lowers the barriers to creation” and doesn’t require coding experience. “With Playground’s conversational interface, you can direct the game just by typing what you want to build,” Google says in a blog post . “Start from a blank canvas, remix starter prompts, or use guided support to shape your concept — and then test it right away. Want to tweak the physics, rewrite the rules, customize the characters, or overhaul the environment? Just ask. You stay in complete control of the creative direction from rough concept to final polish.” When you’re finished making your game, you can share it with a link or publish it to the “Playground Explore gallery” so others can play it. “Select genres” will support in-game leaderboards and multiplayer. The gallery will highlight games that are “fresh, creative, and fun” using ratings and play activity, according to Google. Playground is free to use, but if you have a Google One subscription, you’ll have higher weekly token limits based on your plan, Google spokesperson Nia Carter tells The Verge . Under the hood, Playground is powered by “Google’s existing foundation models (Gemini, Nano Banana, and Lyria) paired with a custom harness refined through our own internally built games and evaluations,” Carter says. Alongside today’s Playground announcement, Google and Unity are also revealing Unity Spark , an AI game-making experience that’s closer to a professional-level game development engine and allows you to create games simultaneously with others. Games made with Unity Spark will be shareable on Playground. A closed beta for Spark is scheduled to kick off later this year, and people who are interested can get on a waitlist starting today. Google’s news today follows Meta’s recent announcement that it will let users build games with AI on their phones and on the web for its Horizon platform with new apps rolling out in early access. Published games made with those tools will be able to be recommended on Facebook and Instagram, which could give them more reach than they would have just being on Horizon. Roblox has also started letting users make games with AI on their phones as part of a “Build” feature that’s in public alpha testing in a few countries.

stories.title: Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen Review
stories.summary: An engrossing expansion full of interesting new characters and vibrant enemies.

sources.name: IGN
sources.title: Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen Review
sources.text: The first Dark Arisen expansion for the original Dragon’s Dogma has a well-lauded place in video game history as the expansion that “fixed” the base game, sanding down the rough technical edges and tweaking things to make the notoriously obtuse RPG more approachable. It also added hours of new content, spiraling an already heady story directly into the heavens on the back of dragon wings. Dark Arisen 2 isn’t as transformational as the first one was, primarily because many of Dragon’s Dogma 2’s biggest issues have been fixed through incremental patching since it came out in 2024. But the new content here definitely flies in the same ambitious skies as its predecessor, pushing the story and world design to new heights, even if some of the new progression options get left behind. As with Dragon’s Dogma 2’s base campaign, Dark Arisen 2’s story remixes themes from the first game without being a simple retelling. Like in the first, another Arisen has been rumored to exist, something that shouldn’t be possible and demands your immediate attention. This takes you north to the frozen mountains of Norgan, a place that is largely abandoned save for the single settlement at its border (and the steady stream of visitors coming from other lands to investigate what’s been lost under all that ice besides you). The expansion’s story also meanders in similar ways to the base game, with plot points getting sidetracked by little tasks or other happenings, but it didn’t feel as distracting since a lot of the “help me and I’ll help you” quests are relegated to side stories. As a whole, this roughly 20-hour main quest is solid, lacking in nuanced writing or ground breaking storytelling but bursting with a tangibly broody mood, big moments, and some genuinely interesting lore. It’s meditation on how a hero of destiny chooses their fate (if they get a choice at all) is unsubtle, and spends far too long at the end really sending the message home, but it sticks it. For those who don’t mind a lot of filler with their killer, there are plenty of people with tasks thoroughly less vital to the survival of reality that need doing. A couple of those quest lines stand out – one where you help the son of the village’s leader become brave and tough enough to follow in his footsteps, for example – but most are just a flimsy excuse to run around the world and beat up enemies. The frigid Norgan region is delightfully dense with things to find and see even if its smaller than most other regions in Dragon’s Dogma 2. What it lacks in square footage on a map, it gains in a sprawling sense of height that stretches from it’s jagged icy peaks down to winding underground caverns that spread wide and interconnect. Navigating up and down the rocks is a treacherous and daunting road at first, but climbing hooks can be used on specific poles scattered throughout to bridge elevations without the fuss. Combined with how dungeons and caves tended to loop back on themselves, revealing exits or opening doors that served as their own shortcuts into and out of zones, and Dark Arisen 2 felt almost like a Zelda or Metroid game in ways this series never has before. The abundance of portcrystals scattered around the map is another navigational relief. There are more in Norgan than there are in Vermund and Bathall combined, making travelling to different zones far more reasonable than it was in the base game. Note that reasonable doesn’t necessarily mean easier. The portcrystal’s abundance is a practical matter, as ox carts wouldn’t last long in the harsh environments. Norgan’s wintry winds often pick up, turning snowfall into blinding whiteouts that threaten to freeze you to death if you aren’t protected by special winterized gear or new consumables designed to stave off these frost effects for a limited time. These came in abundance pretty regularly so I never felt like my life was in danger out there, but the scrambling effect it has on the minimap and how generally hard it is to see or navigate in real time made them a threat worth waiting out at camp. Norgan’s crumbling castles and snowcapped cliffs are a welcome change of pace from the rolling hills and dense hinterlands of Vermund and he craggy deserts of Bathall. It’s also not all snowy wastes. I was surprised to see a break in the snow drifts when I came across a festering poisonous swamp. It matches thematically in that everything in it is dead (or maybe wishes it was), but areas like that and the crystal caves deep below the mountains subverted my expectations for the region in a welcome way. The bulk of what you’ll find hidden in the snow are Spoils, a new gear type that appears in generic shapes (long weapon, aegis, etc.) at first, but is revealed to be a usable piece of equipment when appraised by one of the new NPCs. Rolling the dice for new gear was not particularly exciting, and it further isolated me from having any real attachment to my equipment in a game that already had an abundance of junk to constantly ignore. There are at least things outside of raw stats to consider, as each piece of gear can potentially have special attributes that grant passive abilities or enhance specific weapon skills – but no single piece of gear stayed in rotation long enough to be something I relied on much, with the deluge of experience points I received strapping a rocket to my leveling almost immediately. I can see how these could fit into an endgame grind, but participating in a lottery in hopes to get incrementally stronger as my levels reaches the mid 100s is the sort of loop that I, like The Arisen, simply don’t have the heart for. New skills and abilities for every vocation can be learned from obelisks that dot the ridges and tundra in Norgan. Each have multiple tiers of offerings, and while the first are available for purchase with rift points immediately, the rest need to be unlocked with offering flames, earned in Dark Arisen 2’s second big campaign: the repeatable 12 Lost Rites dungeons

sources.title: Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen review: um RPG completo e com muitos detalhes na jogabilidade
sources.text: Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen vale a pena para quem gosta de RPG de mundo aberto com sistemas profundos, peões com personalidade própria e horas e mais horas de exploração, e o preço compensa pela quantidade de conteúdo. Mas se você espera gráficos ultrarrealistas, uma história cheia de reviravoltas ou um jogo que explica tudo de mão beijada, prepare-se: aqui o tempo (o seu e o do jogo) é parte da experiência. Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen é a versão completa do RPG de ação da Capcom lançado em 2024, agora acompanhado de uma expansão inédita ambientada na região de Norgan. O pacote chega em 9 de outubro de 2026 para PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S, PC (Steam) e, pela primeira vez, Nintendo Switch 2, plataforma em que testei o jogo. O primeiro Dragon’s Dogma, de 20212, chegou ao PlayStation 3 e ao Xbox 360 em maio daquele ano, dirigido por Hideaki Itsuno, nome que os fãs de ação conhecem de Devil May Cry . A história começa em Cassardis, uma vila de pescadores no ducado de Gransys, quando um dragão ataca, arranca o coração do protagonista e o deixa vivo. A partir dali, você se torna o Arisen, o escolhido destinado a enfrentar a criatura. A grande sacada do jogo, já naquela época, eram os peões: companheiros controlados pela inteligência artificial que você cria, treina e compartilha com outros jogadores. Um peão seu podia acompanhar a aventura de outra pessoa e voltar com conhecimento novo sobre missões e inimigos. Em abril de 2013, a Capcom lançou Dragon’s Dogma: Dark Arisen , uma versão expandida que juntava o jogo original a um conteúdo novo e bem mais difícil: a Bitterblack Isle, uma ilha-masmorra pensada para o pós-jogo. Foi essa edição que manteve a franquia viva por anos, ganhando versões para PC em 2016, PS4 e Xbox One em 2017 e Nintendo Switch em 2019. No meio do caminho, o Japão recebeu ainda o Dragon’s Dogma Online (2015), um spin-off online que nunca saiu de lá e foi encerrado em 2019, e a Netflix lançou uma adaptação em anime em 2020. A sequência demorou mais de uma década para chegar. Dragon’s Dogma 2 foi lançado em 22 de março de 2024 para PS5, Xbox Series X|S e PC. Nele, você volta a ser o Arisen, mas desperta sem memória, enquanto um impostor ocupa o trono do reino de Vermund. O mapa se divide entre Vermund, terra dos humanos, e Battahl, lar dos beastren. O jogo passou de 4 milhões de cópias vendidas até o fim de 2025 sem receber nenhuma expansão, uma lacuna que finalmente foi preenchida agora. Assim como em 2013, o novo Dark Arisen junta o jogo-base a um conteúdo inédito, e não por acaso: a expansão é dirigida por Kento Kinoshita, o mesmo diretor do Dark Arisen original. Segundo a Capcom , a nova campanha leva o Arisen ao norte, para Norgan, uma região gelada abandonada há muito tempo. Lá, ele encontra o Dragão Caído (Fallen Dragon), uma criatura imortal que está sem o próprio coração, e se une a uma personagem misteriosa chamada Eir para investigar os segredos dela. O espelho com o primeiro jogo é claro: se antes era o Arisen quem perdia o coração para um dragão, agora é o dragão quem vaga sem ele. Além da campanha, a expansão traz 12 masmorras de desafio, chamadas Lost Rites, que recompensam com equipamentos raros, e relíquias encontradas na exploração de Norgan, que podem ser avaliadas por NPCs específicos para forjar armas e armaduras mais fortes, algumas com efeitos e habilidades únicas. O editor de personagens também ganhou novos penteados e tatuagens. O visual de Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen não é nada impressionante no Nintendo Switch 2. É o padrão de um RPG desse porte, em que o que importa mais é a mecânica e a história do que gráficos extremamente avançados. Quem chega esperando um espetáculo visual de nova geração vai se decepcionar, mas quem conhece a proposta da série sabe que o foco nunca esteve aí. As cutscenes, por outro lado, são bem feitas e cumprem bem o papel de dar peso aos momentos da história. Joguei no Nintendo Switch 2, no modo portátil, com todas as configurações no máximo. O jogo roda a no máximo 30 FPS, com o FSR 3 Frame Generation ligado. A Capcom confirmou que essa é a primeira vez que usa geração de quadros num jogo de Switch 2: o recurso interpola imagens para chegar a algo equivalente a 60 FPS, e pode ser ligado ou desligado a qualquer momento. Durante a jogatina em si, não percebi travamentos ou dificuldades. O único ponto que me incomodou foram algumas cutscenes que demoraram a entrar, dando a impressão de que o console precisava de mais tempo para carregá-las. O mundo de Dragon’s Dogma 2 é aberto, e você vai aceitando diversas missões ao longo da jornada. E aqui vai o primeiro conselho: cuidado para não acumular missões demais e esquecer as que dependem do tempo. Um exemplo: ao chegar a Vernworth, a capital de Vermund, recebi uma missão para entrar no castelo e encontrar uma pessoa. Só que isso só era para ser feito à meia-noite. Não existe um relógio na tela marcando o prazo, mas também não dá para enrolar e esperar o dia raiar. Essa passagem de tempo influencia diversas situações. Pessoas que ficam num lugar durante o dia podem estar em outro à noite. Para avançar as horas, você pode se hospedar numa pousada ou usar bancos especiais espalhados por alguns locais. A noite tem regras próprias. Você precisa de uma lamparina para enxergar no escuro, o que também ajuda a localizar – e ser localizado pelo – os monstros, e, nas áreas selvagens, encontra criaturas diferentes das que aparecem durante o dia. Até os itens sentem o tempo passar. Uma maçã, por exemplo, pode amadurecer, envelhecer e virar itens diferentes para a combinação de materiais. Os alimentos crus pedem atenção redobrada, para que você não acabe consumindo algo velho ou podre que traga efeitos colaterais. Essa foi a parte em que achei a explicação do jogo mais fraca. Há uma variedade enorme de itens, e você acaba tendo que fazer combinações na sorte para descobrir novos objetos. Na criação de poções, por exemplo, é difícil saber de antemão o que vai sair ao juntar duas erva

sources.title: How The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival Builds a Tactical Brawler
sources.text: Hello everyone. The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival is available now on Xbox Series X|S and PC, and rather than walk you through a feature list, I wanted to talk about the decisions that went into creating it. AMC’s “The Walking Dead” is a world defined by scarcity, tension, and the consequences of every decision. The “All Out War” arc adds another dimension to that foundation: momentum, escalation, and increasingly intense confrontations as the conflict with the Saviors grows. Streets of Survival brings those qualities together through a blend of exploration, resource management, and arcade-inspired brawler combat. Search your surroundings, gather supplies and information, and decide how best to approach the dangers ahead. When conflict erupts, combat delivers the immediacy and intensity the story demands, while keeping every encounter grounded in a larger purpose. You are not simply clearing rooms or fighting toward a score screen. Every confrontation moves you closer to an objective, a character, or a reckoning with the Saviors. Exploration creates tension, resources give decisions weight, and combat provides the payoff, combining into an experience built around the escalating conflict at the heart of The Walking Dead’s All Out War. Rick, Daryl and Michonne are not three skins over one moveset. Each has a signature weapon, a separate set of animations and their own skill tree that you invest in every level, which means the same encounter requires a different strategy depending on the selected character. Rick relies on his magnum: long-range firepower that turns every fight into an ammo-management problem. Michonne thrives in close quarters, cutting through hordes with her katana and rewarding you for staying inside the danger. Daryl uses his crossbow to thin threats from a distance before diving in to finish the rest, which makes him the most positional of the three. The levels are tailored around the character meant to play them, creating an experience that adjusts to that character’s available weapons and abilities and giving more freedom in the design, while delivering a custom puzzle for players to solve in each situation. The second big design decision was to stop treating enemies as one mass enemy. Walkers are pressure. They overwhelm through volume and they punish anyone who stands still. The Saviors are opposition: they block, they fire from a distance, and they will happily use walker hordes as cover while they line up a shot. Because both are on screen at once, you are never solving a single problem. That separation exists to change the verb of the combat. In a classic brawler the verb is clear. Here I wanted it to be control: funnel the walkers into a narrow path, isolate the Saviors before they regroup, and save the ammo you’ll need for the targets that actually call for it. The environments are part of that same system rather than a backdrop. Each rewards a different approach, and each one can be turned into a weapon or cost you a health bar if you move through it carelessly. Face enemies between them, lure them into more favorable positions to fight, or use your surroundings in your favor. Giving you different approaches to the same situations was an exciting challenge. Reaching the end credits is where the second design pass starts paying off, as you now have the option to play levels with any character, including the unlockable Negan. Each playable character’s skill tree branches, so a second run with the same survivor is a different build, and playing the same level with a different survivor creates a totally different game. The higher difficulty settings are not damage multipliers: they turn chaotic encounters into tactical puzzles where positioning is the only thing that keeps you alive. Whether you’re returning with a different survivor, experimenting with a new skill path or pushing into higher difficulties, the goal is for every run to ask you to approach the apocalypse differently. The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival is available now on Xbox Series X|S and PC.

sources.title: Gears of War: E-Day – 6 dicas para sobreviver à primeira noite de Emergência
sources.text: Hoje marca o lançamento mundial de Gears of War: E-Day , já disponível no XBOX Series X|S, XBOX no PC, Game Pass e Steam. Uma das sagas mais icônicas de XBOX retorna ao ponto onde tudo começou, levando os jogadores de volta às primeiras horas do Dia da Emergência e ao evento catastrófico que mudou para sempre o mundo de Sera. Gears of War: E-Day nos transporta de volta às primeiras horas da invasão Locust, quando um mundo desprevenido é brutalmente lançado no caos à medida que monstros emergem do subsolo. Ao longo de três dias e noites angustiantes, Marcus Fenix, Dom Santiago e seus destemidos novos companheiros de esquadrão lutam desesperadamente para sobreviver ao ataque que consome a cidade de Kalona, enquanto descobrem a verdadeira dimensão de uma ameaça diferente de tudo o que eles — ou a humanidade — já enfrentaram. Desde o início do prólogo, Gears of War: E-Day oferece uma verdadeira aula de ação e terror. Este não é o inimigo Locust que você já enfrentou antes. Eles são tão astutos quanto violentos e, francamente, você deveria ter medo de encará-los. Seja esta a sua primeira missão ou o seu retorno da aposentadoria para lutar na guerra que está por vir, nós ajudamos você a se preparar. Antes de sair pelas ruas de Kalona, confira algumas dicas que todo Gear precisa saber. 1 – Saiba quando se movimentar ou sair da p**ra do caminho Gears of War é conhecido por ser um jogo de tiro por cobertura, e você dependerá dela para continuar vivo enquanto avança contra os Locust. Mantenha a cabeça baixa, mova-se de uma cobertura para outra e evite sair em campo aberto, a menos que esteja partindo para cima de um inimigo com um ataque corpo a corpo. Mesmo um pequeno grupo de Drones pode causar um dano enorme enquanto você estiver exposto, o que pode trazer problemas tanto para você quanto para o companheiro de esquadrão que talvez precise vir reanimá-lo. Às vezes, a melhor opção é manter a posição com paciência e eliminar os inimigos conforme eles se aproximam — e não há vergonha alguma nessa estratégia. Em outros momentos, você simplesmente precisará correr com tudo e se manter o mais móvel possível — algo que aprendi rapidamente durante um confronto inicial com um Brumak empunhando uma terrível arma de corrente. Nessa situação, não há segurança atrás de uma cobertura: espalhem-se, mantenham a criatura distraída e torçam para que ela não decida investir contra você enquanto sua arma estiver emperrada. Cada arma que você encontrará em E-Day é mais adequada a determinadas situações, o que proporciona uma ótima experiência tática. A Lancer com Motosserra é uma excelente opção versátil, oferecendo poder de fogo a curta e média distância e um carregador enorme — que pode ser aprimorado — para você esvaziar. A Gnasher é uma escopeta excepcional, perfeita para causar dano devastador à queima-roupa. O rifle de precisão Longshot , um dos meus favoritos, dispara projéteis potentes e precisos contra inimigos desavisados a grandes distâncias. Além de ser extremamente satisfatório todas as vezes, isso permite causar uma boa quantidade de dano a inimigos mais resistentes — como um Boomer — antes que eles se aproximem. Também há depósitos espalhados por Kalona que permitem alterar seu conjunto de armas, então não pense que ficará preso para sempre a um estilo específico de jogo. Varie sua estratégia, troque de função com seus amigos e, acima de tudo, experimente! 3 – Combate corpo a corpo é o melhor amigo de um Gear Eu sei que disse que este é um jogo de tiro por cobertura, mas, às vezes, você precisará recorrer a medidas mais pessoais. Antes mesmo de E-Day permitir que você encoste em uma arma, o jogo oferece um curso intensivo de combate corpo a corpo — uma das habilidades mais úteis e capazes de salvar a vida de um Gear. Dedique algum tempo para entender como esse sistema funciona ao empunhar um cano de metal e a pistola Snub: sinta o peso do golpe e como é atingir inimigos à sua frente e, mais importante, atrás de você. Mais adiante, o combate corpo a corpo fica ainda mais divertido com a Lancer com Motosserra, e você se sentirá muito mais confiante ao usá-la depois de dominar os fundamentos dos golpes. 4 – Atirar sem mirar está de volta e continua eficaz Assim que você coloca a cabeça para fora para mirar, transforma-se em um verdadeiro ímã de balas, praticamente convidando todos os inimigos armados no mapa a estourá-lo como um balão. Felizmente, os Gears podem atirar sem mirar por trás da cobertura, uma excelente maneira de causar dano adicional a algo que esteja se aproximando demais. Se você não tiver vida suficiente para avançar e realizar uma finalização corpo a corpo, ou precisar de alguns segundos para se recuperar, atirar sem mirar a partir da cobertura pode ser a jogada decisiva para dar conta do recado. 5 – Fique de olho em missões paralelas e suas recompensas Embora a campanha de E-Day seja predominantemente linear, Kalona conta com grandes áreas abertas que oferecem vários caminhos até o próximo objetivo, além de rotas alternativas que podem levar a missões paralelas. Esses são objetivos menores e opcionais que permitem apoiar outros esquadrões, ajudar civis e contribuir de outras formas para salvar a cidade. Além de oferecerem mais contexto sobre a história como um todo, essas missões também rendem boas recompensas, geralmente uma modificação de arma. 6 – Um sinal sonoro indica itens colecionáveis Enquanto explora, fique atento a um som agudo sempre que entrar em uma nova área da cidade — seja dentro de um edifício ou em uma rua lateral. Isso significa que há um item colecionável por perto. Eles variam de itens conhecidos, como armaduras e identificações da CGO, a objetos inusitados, como… uma lata de sopa. Todos também incluem ótimos pequenos registros de história, alguns escritos pelos próprios integrantes do esquadrão. Essa é uma maneira excelente de conhecer melhor suas histórias e o mundo ao redor, então colete-os sempre que puder. Agora que você já conhece o básico, resta apenas uma c
